library.title: Masters of Camouflage
library.synopsis: A look at animals that use color, pattern, and behavior to disappear from predators and prey alike.

facts.text: Octopuses change both color and skin texture in under a second using specialized cells called chromatophores.
Stick insects don't just look like twigs — some sway gently to mimic branches moving in the wind.
Chameleons primarily change color to communicate mood and temperature regulation, not just camouflage.

library.title: Deep Ocean Giants
library.synopsis: Exploring the largest creatures in the deep sea and how they survive crushing pressure and total darkness.

facts.text: Anglerfish use a bioluminescent lure grown from a modified dorsal spine to attract prey in total darkness.
Giant squid have the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, up to 27 cm across, to catch faint light.
Many deep-sea animals have gelatinous, low-density bodies that resist being crushed by pressure.

library.title: The Solar System, Up Close
library.synopsis: A tour of our solar system's planets and moons, and what makes each one distinct.

facts.text: Saturn's rings are made almost entirely of water ice, with particles ranging from dust to house-sized chunks.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm that has been raging for at least 190 years.
A day on Venus is longer than its year — it rotates once every 243 Earth days but orbits the Sun in 225.

library.title: Built to Survive: Desert Life
library.synopsis: How animals and plants endure extreme heat and scarce water in the world's driest places.

facts.text: A camel's hump stores fat, not water — the fat is metabolized to produce water when needed.
Fennec foxes have oversized ears that radiate body heat, helping them stay cool without sweating much.
Saguaro cacti can absorb and store over 200 liters of water after a single heavy rain.
